content_units: Practical Home-Care Checklist for a Mild Cold
- Encourage rest, regular fluids, and normal meals if possible.
- Use warm tea, broth, or water frequently to keep the throat moist.
- Try salt-water gargles 3-4 times daily for sore throat.
- Use a cool-mist humidifier or steamy shower for congestion.
- Saline nasal spray or saline rinse can help loosen nasal mucus.
- Honey in tea or by spoon can help dry cough if he is not avoiding it for sugar control; use a small amount.
- Keep monitoring for fever, breathing changes, worsening cough, or reduced fluid intake.
- Continue metformin as prescribed unless a clinician advises otherwise.
Common OTC Options for Congestion, Sore Throat, and Dry Cough
Symptom/Need   Common OTC option   Typical practical use   Diabetes-related note
Sore throat or aches     Acetaminophen     Often used for throat pain or body aches   Usually preferred over sugary combination cold drinks; follow package dosing
Nasal congestion     Saline nasal spray/rinse     Good first choice for stuffy nose   No blood sugar effect
Nasal congestion     Oxymetazoline nasal spray     May help short-term congestion relief   Use only as labeled, usually no more than 3 days to avoid rebound congestion

Runny nose/sneezing     Antihistamine   such as cetirizine or loratadine   More helpful if allergy-type symptoms are present   Usually low impact on glucose, but some products are combined with decongestants
Dry cough     Dextromethorphan     Common cough suppressant   Choose sugar-free if available
Mucus/thick secretions     Guaifenesin     Helps thin mucus if cough becomes productive   Drink extra water; choose sugar-free if available
Sore throat     Lozenges or throat sprays     Temporary throat relief   Many lozenges contain sugar; look for sugar-free versions
Diabetes-Specific Double-Checks and What to Avoid
- Prefer   single-symptom products   instead of “cold and flu” multi-symptom combinations.
- Look for   sugar-free   syrups, lozenges, and cough drops when possible.
- Be cautious with   decongestants   such as pseudoephedrine or phenylephrine:
- They can sometimes raise blood sugar.
- They may also raise blood pressure or cause jitteriness/palpitations.
- They are often worth avoiding unless clearly needed and a pharmacist says they are appropriate.
- Double-check labels for hidden combinations like “DM,” “D,” or “severe cold” formulas.
- If he has any kidney disease, liver disease, high blood pressure, heart rhythm issues, prostate enlargement, glaucoma, or trouble urinating, check with a pharmacist before using OTC cold medicines.
- Avoid taking more than one product with the same ingredient, especially   acetaminophen   or   dextromethorphan  .
- Penicillin allergy does   not   usually affect OTC cold medicine choice, but it matters if a clinician later considers antibiotics.
When He Should Contact a Clinician Promptly
- Symptoms are getting worse instead of slowly improving after a few days.
- Fever develops or he starts feeling significantly more ill.
- New wheezing, chest pain, or any shortness of breath appears.
- He has trouble drinking, vomiting, or signs of dehydration.
- Blood sugars are running unusually high or low compared with his normal pattern.
- Cough becomes persistent, more severe, or starts producing significant mucus.
- Sore throat becomes severe, he has trouble swallowing, or there is neck swelling.
- Symptoms last beyond about 7-10 days or seem to improve and then worsen again.
- He tests positive for COVID-19 or has a known flu/COVID exposure and is higher risk due to age and diabetes.
